method: Hand computation from this vector's input.json and conventions.json together with docs/CONVENTIONS.md and the METRIC_DEFINITIONS in src/types.ts. No metric-computing code was written, imported or run, and no expected.json was opened while this file was produced.
rounding: Half-up to four decimal places; terminating values left exact.

warnings.detail: No worker receives any complementary or variable component, so the female and male component figures are both zero. Metrics (b) and (d) report 0 rather than null: there is genuinely no difference between the two figures, and a null would claim the difference is unknown.

working.step0_payDefinition: BASE basic, BONUS complementary_variable, nothing excluded — but every BONUS is 0. Total pay therefore equals BASE for every worker, which makes metrics (a) and (c) identical whichever way the component-scope ambiguity is resolved. That is a useful accident: this is the one vector where that fork cannot bite.
working.step2_sexSplit: Three women (w01, w02, w03) and three men (w04, w05, w06). n = 6, all mapped, excludedN 0. One category, Retail.
working.step4_metricB: Female BONUS mean 0. Male BONUS mean 0. The difference is 0 and the denominator is 0, so the percentage expression is degenerate: 0 divided by 0. ENGINE_CODES.COMPONENTS_ALL_ZERO settles it — the metric reports 0, not null, because there IS no difference between the two figures and a null would assert that the difference is unknown. Reported 0 with W_COMPONENTS_ALL_ZERO.
working.step5_metricC: Both headcounts are ODD at three, so lower_of_two is not reached. Female ascending 2400, 2600, 2800 -> middle 2600. Male ascending 2800, 3200, 3600 -> middle 3200. (3200-2600)/3200 = 0.1875 -> 18.75. Identical to metric (a) because each sex's three values are symmetric about their own mean.
working.step6_metricD: Female BONUS median 0, male BONUS median 0. Degenerate in the same way as metric (b): reported 0 with W_COMPONENTS_ALL_ZERO.
working.step7_metricE: NOT ONE of the six workers receives a complementary or variable component, so 0 of 3 women and 0 of 3 men receive one. The scalar is 0. This zero is of a different kind from the zeros in (b) and (d): those are degenerate differences rescued by a named code, whereas this one is an ordinary, fully defined proportion that simply happens to be zero. Neither is null, and the report must not swap them.

step8_quartiles.sizes: n = 6 gives 6 = 4 x 1 + 2. Under to_lower: sizes 2, 2, 1, 1. Boundaries fall after positions 2, 4 and 5.
step8_quartiles.tie: w03 F and w04 M share the pay level 2800 at positions 3 and 4. With sizes 2, 2, 1, 1 BOTH sit inside Q2, so the tied block does not straddle a boundary and quartileTieRule never has to fire. Worth stating explicitly, because a tie is only a problem when a quarter boundary cuts through it.

composition.Q1: w01 F, w02 F -> 100 percent female
composition.Q2: w03 F, w04 M -> 50 percent female

step8_quartiles.scalarChosen: 100, the female share of the lowest quartile pay band.

working.step9_metricG: One category, Retail, holding all six workers, so the category gap equals metric (a) at 18.75.
working.step10_suppression: minGroupSize null: no suppression, no unreliability.
working.step11_art10: Retail at 18.75 clears the five-point trigger and is flagged. Note that the component gap of 0 does not offset it — Art. 10(1) tests the category's pay gap, not an average of the report's metrics.

ambiguities.issue: Whether W_COMPONENTS_ALL_ZERO also attaches to metric (e), whose value is likewise zero.
readings: Yes — all three zero-valued metrics arise from the same fact about the data.
No — the code names a degenerate percentage expression, and metric (e) has no degeneracy: 0 of 6 is an ordinary proportion.
ambiguities.why: The code's own documentation describes a difference of zero over a denominator of zero. Metric (e) divides 0 by 6, which is perfectly well defined. Attaching the warning there would suggest metric (e)'s zero is a rescued value rather than a true one, which is the precise confusion this vector exists to prevent. Recorded because nothing in the convention document scopes the code to particular metrics.

ambiguities.issue: Whether EngineWarning entries are report-level or per-metric. The type puts warnings on EngineReport, but two metrics here are degenerate for the same reason.
readings: One report-level entry naming both metrics.
ambiguities.chosen: One report-level entry naming both metrics
ambiguities.why: EngineReport.warnings is a flat array on the report with no metric key in EngineWarning, so a per-metric entry could not say WHICH metric it belongs to except in its prose. The detail string names (b) and (d) explicitly. If per-metric attribution matters to a consumer, EngineWarning needs a metric field — a contract question, not a vector question.

ambiguities.issue: Metric (e) is a two-sided proportion carried in a one-scalar MetricValue.
readings: The overall proportion receiving a component.
The percentage-point difference between the two proportions.
ambiguities.chosen: The overall proportion receiving a component
ambiguities.why: This is the vector that decides the fork. Under the difference reading metric (e) would be 0 here AND 0 in all nine other vectors, so this vector's stated purpose — showing that the proportion receiving components is a legitimate zero rather than a missing value — would be indistinguishable from every other case. Under the proportion reading it is 0 here and 100 elsewhere, and the contrast is real.

ambiguities.issue: Metric (f) is eight numbers carried in a one-scalar MetricValue.
ambiguities.chosen: The female share of the lowest quartile pay band
